Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Tuesday, 20 February 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 006)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting_
Mr Dan Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Lachlan Gyles SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health
Mr Neale Dawson with Ms Laura Toose for NSW Nurses and
Midwives' Association

<NICHOLAS MORRIS HOWSON, on former affirmation: [10am]
THE COMMISSIONER: You are on your oath from yesterday,
Mr Howson.
Yes, Mr Fuller.
MR FULLER: Thank you, Commissioner.
<EXAMINATION BY MR FULLER CONTINUING:
MR FULLER: Q. Mr Howson, we finished up yesterday
looking at paragraph 16 of your statement, where you were
referring to an email from Ms Wright. Can you just explain
how it came about that you received that email?
A. Yes. So in my role as the president of the New South
Wales nurses and midwives' branch there, I get a lot of
input from members and other people across the district,
simply because of the role that I'm in, and I am aware of
the policies and procedures surrounding these things.
And we knew those duress alarms that were installed at
the then Bungarribee House unit, which would then later
become the B22 unit at Blacktown Hospital, would be the
same alarms that we would be having at Cumberland Hospital,
so just out of courtesy and comradeship, they let us know
that these new alarms that were installed, they were having
issues with them at the time and to let us get ahead and
perhaps see if we could address these issues in the rollout
that would happen at Cumberland in the near future.
Q. When did you find out about this issue, do you recall?
A. At the time it happened, which is dated in that email,
in the March 2021, from Eliza, we were pretty much kept up
to date as it was happening, including the then SafeWork
investigation into those alarms.
Q. You personally were kept up to date about it; is that
right?
A. Yeah, by the members out at Blacktown, yes.
Q. Can I ask that you have a look at annexure E, please,
which is a copy of the email. I will just ask for that to
be shown on the screen as well.
A. Yes, I have it here.
Q. I take it you don't have any personal experience of

the things raised in this email, but they were communicated
to you at the time; is that right?
A. No, at Bungarribee House, I do not - not personally,
no.
Q. Just having a look at the individuals who received
this email, do you recognise any of those names?
A. Yes, I recognise pretty much all those names still,
apart from Al Owaimrin.
Q. Can you just identify the positions of the individuals
who received these.
A. Sure. So the Arti Kumar, was a registered nurse and
an HSR at Bungarribee House. Julia Norcott was the nurse
unit manager at the time. Sukhpreet Singh was one of the
other nurse managers there, one of the clinical nurse
managers. Shivani Singh was another HSR and Crispen
Mupedzi was another HSR at the time in Bungarribee House.
Q. Was there anyone on this email at the district level
or was it just individuals at Bungarribee House level?
A. I believe this was an internal discussion with the
unit manager at Bungarribee House, who would have then
escalated it outside for hopeful resolution.
Q. The email, just in the last sentence, refers to a PIN
notice given by SafeWork. Do you know what a PIN notice
is?
A. It should actually read "improvement notice" because
it was issued by SafeWork not by an HSR, in that regard,
but there yes, was an improvement notice issued by
Inspector Megan May regarding the duress alarms at
Bungarribee House.
Q. A PIN notice is a provisional improvement notice?
A. Yes, a provisional improvement notice, yeah.
Q. That and would normally be issued by a HSR --
A. Correct.
Q. -- a health and safety representative -- -
A. Correct, yeah.
Q. -- rather than by --
A. Yes, they're generally reviewed by an inspector and
either dismissed or made into an improvement notice, yeah.

Q. In this case, you're aware that an improvement notice
was --
A. Correct.
Q. -- in fact, issued?
A. -- issued directly by a SafeWork Inspector.
Q. Have you seen a copy of that improvement notice?
A. At the time, yes, I was unable to find one in the
short time frame for providing evidence for this Inquiry.
Q. I see. Do you know whether the issues raised in this
email were escalated up to LHD management?
A. I'm unaware at the time if it made it all the way to
LHD management but as the alarms were an LHD decision,
I would have assumed that they made it up to there at some
point.
Q. Do you know whether the improvement notice from
SafeWork made its way to LHD management?
A. Yes. All improvement notices are sort of managed at
a district level.
Q. How do you know that?
A. Experience with other improvement notices in the
service issued directly to me as well as other senior
executive members.
Q. So based on your knowledge of the usual practice --
A. Yes.
Q. -- with improvement notices, you would assume this
improvement notice made its way to LHD management, although
you don't know that for sure?
A. Yeah. So improvement notices are generally issued to
the person conducting the business, and a representative,
a worker, an HSR or someone in the workplace where it
occurred, and it's generally some sort of higher level
executive like director of people and culture or the CE
themselves who gets a copy issued to them.
Q. Are you aware of any specific response to this
improvement notice?
A. No, I am not. That would be sitting with SafeWork.
Q. I think the next event chronologically in your
statement is at paragraph 20. If I can just ask that to be

shown on the screen, please.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. In paragraph 20, you talk about testing your alarm at
the start of a shift on 25 February 2022. Based on your
answers yesterday, I take it that was shortly after you
personally first started using the duress alarm?
A. Correct.
Q. But that's the AiRISTA duress alarm; is that right?
A. (Witness nods).
Q. You say that the self-test function didn't work. Can
you just explain what you mean by that?
A. So as I mentioned yesterday when we had the picture up
of the alarms, pressing the blue button on that style of
alarm initiates what the manufacturer calls a "self-test".
You end up getting a message on the alarm that just says,
"Self-test succeeded."
It doesn't really give you any feedback on what it's
testing, whether it is testing connectivity, functionality
of the three alarm modes, being man down, pull cord or
button press. It doesn't really give you much feedback at
all other than, yes, you've pressed a button; yes, you've
got battery.
Q. And so in this case, you did the self-test but it
didn't say that it was successful?
A. Nothing happened, and then when - I guess, as the
paragraph says, the pull cord didn't function, the man down
didn't work and the button trigger didn't alert either
after that self-test failed.
Q. I'll just go through each of those if I can. So the
pull tag function didn't work? Can you just explain,
firstly, what you --
A. That's the pull tag function where it's attached to
your clothing. I know the image isn't up at the moment,
but there is a tag on the top, and as soon as you pull it
a little clip pulls down and the alarm goes off. It's one
of the more surreptitious methods of triggering your alarm
so people don't notice. It doesn't give any feedback to
you other than a slight click, and it certainly doesn't
give any feedback to anybody else around, so it's a nice
little way to call for help. It's just a quick
(indicating) and you're done.

The other one on there is the man down alarm which is,
as it says, when there's no movement or the alarm is not in
a vertical position, it will sound a brief warning and then
if the alarm doesn't get cancelled within five - I think
it's about five seconds, it will trigger. And then the
button alarm is the button alarm. You press the button, it
goes off.
Q. What did you do to test the pull tag?
A. I just pulled it. I pulled the tag and the alarm
separately, so physically in front of me.
Q. And nothing happened; is that right?
A. No. I observed the click that indicated it had been
pulled and there was no response.
Q. So you heard the click but no response?
A. No. No other alarms nearby that anybody else was
wearing went off, my alarm didn't give any feedback, and
there was nothing.
Q. So both the case that, to your knowledge, the alarm
didn't notify anyone else and obviously there was no
response; is that right?
A. Yeah, that's right. No response.
Q. The man down alarm, how did you test that?
A. I held it flat in my hand, indicating that it was
horizontal rather than vertical, and I also put it on the
desk.
Q. And to your knowledge, that didn't notify anyone else;
is that right?
A. No, it did not.
Q. What would normally happen if the man down alarm is
working? Would you be able to see on the device that
something has happened?
A. Yeah, as it commonly does accidentally go off if
you're sitting down or if it's in a wrong spot or if you're
leaning back in your chair a bit far or whatever you're
doing, it gives you a brief warning. It says, "Are you
okay", and you have to dismiss the "Are you okay" by
pressing one of the buttons - I can't remember off the top
of my head, it is a bit of muscle memory at this point -
and then it dismisses that warning.

Q. And the button alarm, I take it, you attempted to
press it for five seconds?
A. Yes.
Q. And nothing happened; is that right?
A. And no response, no.
Q. You say that you report those issues to the nurse
manager; is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. You submitted an ims+ report. What is an ims+ report?
A. It is the incident management system that NSW Health
uses across the state to record any and all incidents from
clinical incidents to work health safety incidents to
corporate incidents. Anything that isn't clinical is
pretty much recorded in the ims+ system.
Q. Why did you submit an ims+ report on this occasion?
A. It is the standard procedure for any sort of incident
to be recorded as part of our incident reporting policy.
Q. Can I ask you to have a look at annexure F, please,
and for that to be put on the screen?
A. Sure. What is F? They are not titled "Annexure" in
here.
Q. Do you have numbers in your folder rather than --
A. No.
Q. I will just try to find the number to assist. Do you
have a number 45 - tab number 45?
A. Yes, thank you.
Q. Thank you. You recognise that as an ims+ report; is
that right?
A. That is an ims+ report. So that's the version that
you can get after you submit an ims+ and you can print
a copy for your own records.
Q. So the ims+ system is a sort of electronic form; is
that right?
A. It is.
Q. And this is the print-out of that form?
A. Yeah.

Q. There's no name on this version of the form. Are you
confident that you submitted this ims+ report?
A. Yeah. You, at the time, can only see incident reports
that you submit, unless you're a manager of an area, so any
ims+ that you have access to as a user is one you
submitted.
Q. So you wouldn't have been able to print out this ims+
report if it wasn't one that you submitted?
A. No, so this is - and I can also say this would be mine
because it is in the unit that I worked in at the time,
which is notified on the second page, the Hainsworth unit
at the top.
Q. If we just have a look at the second page, about
halfway down, there's a heading that says. "What
happened?" And then "Details"?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. And do you see there the first four items of are the
four things you have identified --
A. Yes.
Q. -- in the paragraph of your statement that we just
looked at?
A. That's correct.
Q. You say "duress alarm system not functioning". Did
you mean anything more by that?
A. Simply that mine didn't work and then after doing that
report none of the others worked, which sort of led me to
conclude that the system was not working at all. A few
phone calls, I believe, were made to other units, "Hey, are
your tags working?" And the answer was, "No, we
self-tested and got nowhere", and then I thought, "All
right, well, I'll do an incident report and flick it up the
line."
Q. So did you test other tags?
A. No, I just rang. I rang. It's a standard procedure
for everybody to be able to test those alarms and I would
trust any response from my colleagues, if I asked, "Are
your alarms testing or working", and if they said, "No",
they would have gone through the same process that I did.
Q. Just so I understand, after you tested your alarm, you

asked other people whether --
A. Yes.
Q. -- theirs were working and they said they weren't?
A. So I would have - I immediately asked the people in my
unit as well as checking some of the other units.
Q. If we have a look at the bottom of this page, there's
a line that says "Initial harm score", and the number is 3.
Can you just explain, is that on a scale?
A. Yeah, there's four harm scores now, 1 to 4, with 1
being the most serious and 4 being the least serious. It's
calculated by the things that you choose. It's not a user
input number.
Q. Do you know what inputs would have resulted in a harm
score of 3?
A. So there's things directly above that, would
have pretty - my understanding is the way the assessment
options are selected is what the harm score comes out to.
Three and 4s are generally managed at a unit level; 1s and
2s are managed at a hospital or district level.
For reference, a harm score 1 is something that leads
to, you know, a serious adverse event like a death or
permanent disablement, problems with surgery, et cetera,
big clinical risks - things like that. 2s, serious injury
with no, you know, long-term lasting damage, and 3s and 4s
are missed medication, slips, trips and falls, people
absconding, things like that.
Q. Would you agree with a harm score of 3 in relation to
this incident?
A. Whilst it is more serious than a 3 would indicate,
it's a report for that unit, because I was - you're unable
to report at a higher level than to your direct manager
when you do these incident reports. So when the system
looks at it, when you're saying it needs a local management
response only, that's because you're escalating to your
manager and they're escalating up.
So I would have assumed that it should have at least
been a 2, because it is not just a unit, it was a hospital,
and at that point it did turn out to be a district-wide
issue, so that would indicate a much higher harm score
should have been assigned, but it is again a limitation of
the system itself.

Q. Do you know who received this ims+ report?
A. So a copy is generally sent - an email notification
gets sent to your immediate line manager and the clinical
governance unit also has overview of all incident reports
coming in for your sort of management structure that you
are in. So that would be the Cumberland Hospital mental
health service level.
Q. And your immediate manager would have been the nurse
unit manager?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you receive any feedback in response to this
report?
A. Yeah, a few phone calls saying, "You tested and
they're not working?" I was like, "Yep", they're like,
"All right, we'll look into it" because the nurse managers
up the chain also receive copies of it and if they're in
front of a computer, they'll get an email notification that
an incident report was submitted.
Q. Who did you receive phone calls from?
A. I couldn't tell you the individual but I could tell
you the role at the time. It would have been one of our
either acute nurse manager or the recovery nurse manager,
one of those people in those roles is sort of responsible
for the day-to-day running of the clinical incidents for
that shift that they're on. So they're sort of the point
of escalation before it goes from the clinical setting to
an executive setting like a deputy director or a director.
Q. Do you know whether this issue was escalated beyond
those managers?
A. I do believe it went up to district because Digital
Health Solutions got involved to let us know that, yes,
there was an IT breakdown at that point, and I think that's
in one of the emails further down.
Q. What was the outcome of Digital Health Solutions
getting involved?
A. In this particular incident, I think it was down for
about 24 hours before we got a notification that it was
back up. Although I may be getting confused with the
C4A/C4B issue further down the line, which we haven't got
to the in timeline yet.

Q. But to the best of your memory it was about 24 hours
that the system was down.
A. Yeah.
Q. Did you receive any feedback as to why the system --
A. No.
Q. -- had not --
A. I believe at the time there would have been
a communication for telecommunications breakdown, the
digital health service is generally pretty good at sending
notifications out when certain things aren't functioning.
We get, like, a broadcast across the district.
Q. Did you continue to experience issues with the duress
alarm system at Cumberland Hospital after this incident?
A. Personally, no, because I ended up in higher-grade
duties after that and I was only putting alarms on when
I entered units as I wasn't walking directly on the floor.
And then I also ended up on secondment outside of health
for six months after that.
Q. Did you have other people reporting issues --
A. Yes.
Q. -- with duress alarms?
A. I did.
Q. At Cumberland Hospital during the period?
A. At Cumberland and within the emergency departments
base at Westmead where we also have mental health staff
based.
Q. I'll ask you about the Westmead emergency department.
A. Yes.
Q. If you have a look at paragraph 26 of your statement,
please?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Here you've mentioned concerns being raised by staff
in the Westmead ED in October and November 2022. Are these
the events that you were thinking of when you just gave me
that answer?
A. Yes.
Q. I take it from your earlier answers, you didn't have

any direct involvement in these incidents?
A. No, it was just another member reporting to me that
they were experiencing these issues and not getting much in
the way of information back.
Q. Can you just elaborate on that?
A. So in this - I think these are some of the other
incident reports from the ims+ system that I annexed in
here.
This was a member up in Westmead, who had been
experiencing a personal threat requiring a code black, and
they had relied upon their duress alarm, which was the same
model, and however they triggered it - I couldn't tell you
without going to read the incident report - they did not
get a response and it didn't seem to give any feedback
other than that they had pulled it themselves and didn't
receive any sort of assistance until another method of
calling for help had occurred.
Q. I'll just ask you a couple of questions about the
documents you have attached. If we can have a look at
annexure H, please, and for you, Mr Howson, that's tab 47
A. Tab 47. Yes.
Q. If you just look on the second page?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Which is the substantive email, it's from someone
named Steven Westbrook Sr. Who is that?
A. He was the work health and safety representative who
was working for the district covering the emergency
department space at the time.
Q. In the first paragraph in that email, he refers to the
"MH pod". Do you know what that is?
A. Mental health pod. It's a bit of a colloquial term
for the six-bed space in the Westmead emergency department
where the mental health patients who have been assessed as
having a mental health concern rather than a physical
health concern are bedded until an appropriate ward bed is
found for them.
Q. In the third paragraph, Mr Westbrook says:
I have already briefed Wade Norrie on these
[issues] ...

Do you know who Wade Norrie is?
A. So Wade Norrie was the director of mental health
services - director of nursing for mental health services
at the time this email was sent.
Q. Do you know whether his role related to the Westmead
ED or the Cumberland Hospital or both?
A. Both. Mental health services in Western Sydney Local
Health District are a district-wide service and they have
a district-wide director of nursing, and that was Wade
Norrie at the time.
So working in ED, in that space, it was supposed to be
a collaborative, co-located model of care between both
Westmead and mental health services. So it would have been
both sides getting involved. That would be the general
manager and director of nursing for emergency as well as
a director of nursing and our executive for mental health
services.
Q. And so to your knowledge, Mr Norrie would also have
been responsible for Blacktown; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. Do you know when he started as director of nursing?
A. February 2020 I believe.
Q. So it would have been prior to the rollout of AiRISTA
at Blacktown as well, is that right, to your knowledge?
A. It would have been prior to, but I would imagine it
would have already been in process when he arrived.
Q. Can you just explain how it came about that you were
forwarded this email by Mr Westbrook?
A. I had been doing a lot of work health and safety work
with my role as an HSR and in my capacity as the branch
president there, and I had worked quite closely with Steven
Westbrook, both in his role as a work health safety person
for the mental health service prior to his role as this,
and also worked clinically with him when he was a security
officer in the mental health intensive care unit.
We both share a strong passion for keeping workers
safe, so if we're safe we can provide safe and effective
care, and he said, "I'm not getting much traction with
these issues. My hands are a little bit tied. Here is the

information, do with it what you would normally do", which
is speak to the association and get some help from their
work health and safety officers and come in from - come in
from a different angle.
Q. So it was raised with you in your capacity with the
NSW Nurses and Midwives' Association?
A. Correct.
Q. I will just ask you about the second document you
attached in relation to this, which is annexure I, which
should just be the next tab for you?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Again, this is an email that has been forwarded to
you?
A. Correct.
Q. By Neethu Maria Babu?
A. So Neethu was a nurse working in the mental health pod
space at Westmead Hospital at the time.
Q. That's again the mental health pod in the ED?
A. In the Westmead ED, the co-located space that we
share.
Q. How did it come about that you were emailed about
this?
A. They were again discussing safety concerns and I said,
"Look, we've been working on these for a while as a branch.
If you have a concern that you've put in writing, please
send us a copy so we can put it all together and try and
get some sort of action on this."
Q. In this email, Ms Babu refers to the "acute side". Do
you know what that is?
A. So Westmead ED is divided into acute A and acute B.
It's just a way of dividing the large amount of beds into
two separate teams, and the mental health pod space bridges
both. It is a little corridor between the two, both side A
and side B. So she would have said "acute" as in to leave
the mental health space and go to one of the acute sides.
Unfortunately it doesn't say which side, A or B, but
she would have gone to one of the primary staff stations
there to seek help.

Q. You've also provided an ims+ report, which I won't
ask that you be shown, but relating to these incidents.
I take it that that's not a report that you submitted; it's
again --
A. No.
Q. -- one that was provided to you?
A. Yeah, no, it was provided.
Q. Are you aware of in any response to that ims+ report?
A. So you are allowed to request - yeah, if you look -
actually look at one of them, one of the very last sections
in the ims+ report is a feedback to notifier. When you
submit one, you're allowed to choose yes or no, you want
feedback. Even when you choose yes, you very often get no
feedback in there.
Q. In paragraph 28 --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Sorry, just sticking with that
annexure for a minute, the email?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. From - it is Ms Babu?
A. Correct.
Q. Where it says "I activated the mobile duress and no
staff responded, I pressed the wall mounted one, no staff
responded", do you know, yourself, whether that was because
the alarms didn't work or whether the alarms worked but
no-one responded?
A. It did turn out that the alarms in that situation were
deemed not working. So she had pulled her mobile - meaning
personal - duress, the AiRISTA Flow tag, and then gone to
press a button near where the mental health nurses sit in
that space, and that fixed duress alarm that was labelled
"code black", did not function.
Q. All right. So if neither the fixed one or the mobile
one works, who would be responsible for having them fixed?
A. So that actually is the "Donna Robinson" referred to
in the email there, that's the nurse manager for
education - nurse manager for, sorry, for the emergency
department at Westmead. That fixed code black button was
repaired and deemed working after this.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.

MR FULLER: Q. Do you know whether there was any
response to the issue about the personal duress alarm not
working in this situation?
A. I believe it turned out to be that there was a wi-fi
blind spot in the area where the mental health nurses were
sitting, and that was also rectified after much backwards
and forwards.
Q. You have attached as annexure K a letter that you sent
to Wade Norrie in your capacity as president of the
Cumberland branch of the NSW Nurses and Midwives'
Association, which raises these issues, in summary?
A. Yes.
Q. You say that, to the best of your knowledge, the
branch did not receive a response to that letter; is that
right?
A. To the best of my knowledge, we wouldn't have received
a timely response. We quite often didn't get responses to
correspondence for months at a time.
Q. Do you know whether any response was received to this
letter?
A. I would have to go back and check my records with the
branch secretary. All communication goes through the
branch secretary, not my role as president. I'd have to
double-check with her to see if we ever got an adequate
response to this letter.
Q. Did you have any discussions with Mr Norrie or anyone
else about the subject matter of this letter?
A. None that I would be able to get minutes or - none
that I would be able to get minutes for or any other thing.
They would have been just brief conversations about, "We're
working on it" or "This is where we're up to."
Q. Do you have a recollection of those conversations?
A. Unfortunately no, I don't. They were some time ago
and many things have happened since then.
Q. It sounds like the particular issues that this nurse
experienced were rectified?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you remember how long it took for that to happen?
A. It was not quick. I believe some of them were also

mentioned by Steven Westbrook Sr in that other email about
the fixed duress alarms not working and they were
a follow-up to that situation that Neethu, Ms Babu, had
spoken about in that email.
Q. The next event chronologically is in paragraph 22 of
your statement, if you can just have a look at that,
please.
A. Yes.
Q. You refer there to a resolution passed by the
Blacktown branch of the NSW Nurses and Midwives'
Association. Did you have any involvement in the passing
of that resolution?
A. No, so because we're all a separate list of branches,
Blacktown Hospital has one, Blacktown mental health has
one, Westmead Hospital has one, Cumberland has one, but we
do all work closely together as a district because again,
we are sharing at that level, when you're talking about
hospital-wide issues, you're also sharing a district-wide
executive structure.
So we quite often sort of talk about the larger issues
affecting the hospitals as a group. So it's a group of
union representatives from Mount Druitt Hospital,
Blacktown, Westmead, Westmead Children's, Cumberland and
Auburn hospitals, all speak quite regularly on larger
issues, like violence and aggression, duress alarms,
staffing.
Q. You have provided an email chain relating to this
issue which is annexure G, if you can just have a look at
tab 46, please?
A. Thank you. Yes.
Q. I'll just ask for that to be put on the screen as
well. If we just start at the end of the document,
obviously the email is going backwards in time. At page 5
of the PDF, you see an email there from Kirstie
Kwiatkowski?
A. We just call her KK.
Q. Good. Who is she?
A. So she is the Blacktown branch secretary for the main
hospital at Blacktown, hence the correspondence coming from
her because all correspondence for branches is in and out
via secretaries.

Q. Have you seen a copy of the resolution that was passed

Q. And do HealthShare have a role in escalation of
problems under at least statewide contracts?
A. Sometimes we do raise it up with HealthShare,
especially for if it's a recurring issue, if it is an
ongoing supply issue, especially high specialty items.
I mean, obviously there is not many, or if there is not
many suppliers that are contracted, if it is one of two,
that's obviously an issue, it's definitely an alert, so we
will - those discussions will occur with HealthShare, yes.
Q. You have referred to "specialty items". Those are
items that may not be routinely kept on hand; is that
right, or they are --
A. So specialty items might be kept on hand but only used
by certain specialties; or it might be products that are
only used in, let's say, operations, in operating theatres;
or may be specialty items that are only used by the
anaesthetics; or sometimes we do get occasional, depending
on patients, the surgery and so on, a request for a very
special item that we might not even keep as a regular
supply.
Q. Are they ordered through the same system or is there
a separate system?
A. So they are eventually processed via the same system.
Would you like me to give you an example?
Q. Yes, please.
A. So let's say almost always those will be treated as
loan products, especially if they are prostheses. So let's

say a surgeon needs to use a very special graft for an
unusual case.
Q. Yes.
A. They would probably - and the hospital will probably
be alerted to this case coming through. I assume that
a discussion would have been - between the clinician and
either their head of department, who would then contact
either the director of surgery or the nurse manager to
advise them that this is coming, this case, and we need
this special item, who then will pass on that information
to me to say that this is coming, "What do we need to do,
how can we process it?"

what's the most clinically appropriate and they will
probably do the request for that product with the supplier
or the product specialist, and that product will then be
brought to the hospital on a loan basis. If it is
a product that needs to be resterilised then it will be
delivered to the sterilising department, it will be
processed there ready for use, so then at the procedure
time they will use it.
Q. Yes.
A. If it is a product that we have used before and it has
been in our catalogue, the staff, or the nursing staff,
will be able to scan that product into h-trak and record it
that way. If not, they will wrap up the packaging,
indicate the specific MRN of the patient, procedure, and
bring it to our supply office so that then we can add it to
that patient usage.
So then what happens next is we contact the supplier
and ask for loan pro forma. Upon the issue of the loan
pro forma we ensure that the price which was discussed
previously, the item code, the lot number, is captured
correctly and it matches, and once that is done we
process - we raise a requisition which goes through
iProcurement.

A. Yes.

A. h-trak is our - it is a local system. It is a patient

implant and consumable usage capturing sort of system.

A. Yes.

entering of information into h-trak happens at procedure
time.
Q. I see. So it's done through the - it comes out of
the --
A. So it's, let's say inside a theatre they would

scanners, so they would scan, let's say, the patient's

information from SurgiNet into h-trak. It will bring up
the procedure name, primary procedure list, patient MRN.

entry into h-trak, nursing staff will scan all products
that were used for that patient.

A. Yes.

A. Yes.

A. Yes.

A. Yes.

A. That's correct.

A. Yes.

used on a regular basis in operations, so let's say they
can be ocular lenses. The frequency of use and the need of
a certain range probably calls to have those on
consignment - on a consignment arrangement. So basically
a range of products which has been revised or has been
predetermined by the clinical team or the clinician
themselves - clinicians themselves, the surgeons, would
determine the range of products and the quantity, and then
once that is done, it obviously goes through an approval
process, again through the executive, depending on the
delegation, and then that stock is placed into operating
theatres to be used for future - for whatever is required.
We do have one little process. When consignment is
brought in to the hospital, let's say we've gone through
all the approval process and so on, we determine the

A. Because --

pre-purchase this product it will cost us a lot of money to
keep so much stock on hand.
Q. I see.

unnecessary cost. So I think that's good enough reason to
have this consignment.

use it, or depending on their specialties, whether they
would use or not, and then that product, or that request,
is reviewed at the clinical products committee and then, if
it meets criteria, it might be approved or not.
